## 1. Happiness and income

### Question 1
```{r}

# Load data
ess9 <- haven::read_sas("ess9e02.sas7bdat")
ess9 <- data.frame(ess9)

# Run prep from Bright Space 
source("prepare_ess9.R")

# Create happy_cent first
data_ess9$happy_cent <- data_ess9$happy - mean(data_ess9$happy)

# Store in a list
formulas <- c(
  netincome ~ happy,
  netincome ~ polintr,
  netincome ~ happy + polintr,
  netincome ~ happy * polintr,
  netincome ~ happy_cent + polintr,
  netincome ~ happy_cent * polintr
)

# Make empty lists
models <- vector("list", length(formulas))
summaries <- vector("list", length(formulas))

# Fill them up
for (i in 1:length(formulas)) {
  models[[i]] <- lm(data=data_ess9, formulas[[i]])
  summaries[[i]] <- summary(models[[i]])
}

data.frame(
  model = paste0("reg", 1:6),
  r2 = sapply(summaries, function(s) s$r.squared),
  r2adj = sapply(summaries, function(s) s$adj.r.squared),
  aic = sapply(models, AIC),
  bic = sapply(models, BIC)
)

metrics <- data.frame(
  model = paste("reg", 1:6, sep=""),
  r2 = sapply(summaries, function(s) s$r.squared),
  r2adj = sapply(summaries, function(s) s$adj.r.squared),
  aic = sapply(models, AIC),
  bic = sapply(models, BIC)
)
print(metrics)

```
Best in terms of AIC -> reg3 or reg5 (lowest value is 18040.67)
Best in terms of Best for BIC -> reg3 or reg5 (lowest value is 18070.30) 
Best in terms of R2 -> reg4 or reg6 (highest at 0.0422)
Best in terms of Adjusted R2 -> reg3 or reg5 (highest at 0.0360) -> prefers simpler models


### Question 2
I choose the regression 5 model. It's a winner in the table above together with reg3. While statically equivalent to reg3, it's centered around the average happiness, making it easier to interpret.

```{r}
summary(models[[5]])

ggplot(data_ess9, aes(x=factor(polintr), y=netincome)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(alpha=0.5) +  # show individual points too
  labs(x="Political interest (1=very, 4=not at all)", y="Net income")

ggplot(data_ess9, aes(x=happy_cent, y=netincome)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha=0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method="lm") +
  labs(x="Happiness (centered)", y="Net income")

```
What we can see from the data is that political interest is not a strong statistical predictors for income, in-spite of p < 0.05.
We also see statistically significant positive association between happiness and net income. But R2 is only ~4% and the regression slope is modest, so also it's not a strong predictors for income. This does not directly imply causality (happy people earn more).


## 2. About histograms

```{r}
set.seed(1)
par(mfrow = c(3,3))
for(i in 1:9) {
  mysample = rnorm(20)
  hist(mysample, main = i)
}
```
```{r}
install.packages("cowplot")
set.seed(2)
par ( mfrow = c (1, 1))
mysample = data.frame (measurements = rnorm (200))
p1 = ggplot ( mysample ) + geom_histogram ( aes ( x = measurements ) , bins = 4 )
p2 = ggplot ( mysample ) + geom_histogram ( aes ( x = measurements ) , bins = 20 )
p3 = ggplot ( mysample ) + geom_histogram ( aes ( x = measurements ) , bins = 60 )
p4 = ggplot ( mysample ) + geom_histogram ( aes ( x = measurements ) , bins = 400 )
cowplot::plot_grid(p1 , p2 , p3 , p4 , labels = LETTERS [1:4])
```
